faq.a: Chronic inflammation can mask cancer, so any persistent mass without resolution should be biopsied.
Immunosuppression reduces containment of Mycobacterium, allowing spread to breast tissue.
faq.q: Why is TB mastitis more common in HIV patients?

faq.a: Start empiric antibiotics covering common skin flora; monitor response and consider TB treatment if no improvement.
faq.q: What if I cannot get a culture?

exam: What is the next step after identifying a draining sinus in a diabetic patient? — Obtain FNA for culture and start empiric antibiotics while arranging drainage.

How would you differentiate chronic bacterial mastitis from inflammatory breast cancer at the bedside? — Look for systemic signs of infection, purulent discharge, and lack of peau d'orange; cancer shows firm edema without pus.
A patient with chronic mastitis does not improve after 48 h of antibiotics; what should you consider? — Evaluate for TB mastitis, obtain Ziehl‑Neelsen stain, and consider anti‑TB therapy.
Why are NSAIDs avoided in a patient with chronic mastitis and renal impairment? — NSAIDs can worsen renal function and mask fever, hindering assessment of infection severity.
Explain the role of glycaemic control in managing chronic mastitis. — Hyperglycaemia impairs neutrophil function and wound healing; tight control improves response to antibiotics.
When is incision and drainage indicated in chronic mastitis? — When a fluctuant abscess is palpable or imaging shows a collection larger than 2 cm.
What red‑flag symptom mandates urgent referral to a surgical team? — Signs of sepsis (fever > 38 °C, tachycardia, hypotension) or rapidly expanding necrotic tissue.
How would you counsel a patient to prevent recurrence after healing? — Emphasise breast hygiene, regular self‑examination, optimal diabetes management, and prompt treatment of skin breaches.
ai.title: Chronic Mastitis
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Chronic mastitis is a persistent inflammatory condition of the breast, often due to infection or ductal obstruction, presenting with pain, swelling, and sometimes draining sinuses. In low‑resource settings, common causes include bacterial infection, tuberculosis, and diabetic skin changes.

b: Clinical pattern of chronic pain, swelling, and discharge
Exclusion of malignancy by ultrasound or fine‑needle aspiration if possible
sections.p: A prolonged inflammatory process of the breast tissue lasting >4 weeks, characterised by erythema, induration, tenderness and possible sinus formation. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by imaging and microbiology when available.

b: Mild: localized induration, no systemic signs
Moderate: diffuse induration, low‑grade fever, sinus tract
Severe: extensive necrosis, high‑grade fever, sepsis risk
sections.p: Severity is graded by extent of tissue involvement and systemic response:

b: Bacterial infection (Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus spp.) – most common
Tuberculous mastitis – especially in HIV‑positive patients
Diabetic skin ulceration extending into breast tissue
Fungal infection (Candida) in immunocompromised
Rare: inflammatory breast cancer – must be excluded
sections.p: In East African low‑resource hospitals the hierarchy of causes is:

b: Unilateral involvement in >90% of cases
Sinus tract often located at the nipple‑areolar complex
Fever, malaise in moderate/severe disease
sections.p: Patients report progressive breast pain, warmth, and a palpable hard area. Chronic cases develop draining sinuses that may exude purulent or serous fluid. Systemic symptoms appear only in moderate‑severe disease.
Select tests that answer specific clinical questions; adapt when resources are limited.

t.b: Is there an abscess or solid mass? – Fluid collection suggests abscess; solid mass prompts biopsy
What organism is causing infection? – Growth identifies bacteria; no growth may indicate TB or non‑infective cause
Is Mycobacterium tuberculosis present? – Acid‑fast bacilli confirm TB mastitis
Is diabetes poorly controlled? – High values guide tighter glycaemic control
Is there concurrent pulmonary TB? – Suggests disseminated disease

b: Rapidly enlarging mass with skin retraction – suspect inflammatory carcinoma
High‑grade fever, tachycardia, hypotension – sepsis
Extensive necrosis or foul‑smelling discharge – possible necrotising infection
sections.p: Identify features that demand urgent referral or intervention.

b: Empiric broad‑spectrum antibiotics covering Staph and Strep (e.g., amoxicillin‑clavulanate) while awaiting culture
If TB suspected, start anti‑TB regimen (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) after confirmation
Optimize diabetes control – insulin or oral agents as per local protocol
Incision and drainage of abscesses when fluctuant; pack sinuses with sterile gauze
Analgesia with paracetamol; avoid NSAIDs in renal impairment
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, control inflammation, and support healing.

b: Re‑examine breast weekly until signs resolve
Educate patient on breast hygiene and early reporting of new pain
Screen diabetic patients for skin breakdown
Vaccinate against TB where program exists
sections.p: Regular review to ensure resolution and prevent recurrence.

b: Inflammatory breast cancer – rapid skin changes, firm edema, no pus
Breast abscess – acute, localized, usually without sinus formation
Granulomatous mastitis – sterile granulomas, often in young women
Negative bacterial culture does not rule out TB; consider stain and PCR
Ultrasound may miss early TB lesions; clinical suspicion remains key
Normal glucose does not exclude recent hyperglycaemia; check HbA1c

whenToSeekHelp: High‑grade fever or signs of sepsis
Rapidly enlarging breast mass with skin changes
